1.note: The author is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

The author is using **in the eyes of Yahweh** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the judgment of Yahweh” or “according to what Yahweh approved.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Yahweh was pleased]

The author is using **as time by time** as a common expression of the culture to mean “as he had done on previous occasions.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [as he had done on previous occasions]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **omens**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what the signs would tell him]

The author is using **he set his face to the wilderness** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam turned and looked toward the wilderness. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he turned and looked toward the wilderness]

2.note: The author is using **lifted up his eyes** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balaam looked up and gazed ahead of himself. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And Balaam looked up]
The pronoun **him** refers to Balaam. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [upon Balaam]

3.note: The author is using the phrase **And he lifted up his oracle and said** to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the message that he himself is declaring. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Balaam declares this]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean that he is the son whose father is Beor. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the son whose father is Beor]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the message spoken by the man, that is, by Balaam himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the message that the man whose eye is opened speaks]

The word translated as **opened** represents the written Hebrew text. However, some scholars have proposed that by changing the vowels of this word it would say “closed.” In this case, the meaning would be that Balaam’s eyes had previously been closed. You may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [having been closed of the eye]

Here Balaam is speaking of his ability to perceive what God reveals as if it were physical sight, describing himself as **opened of the eye**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who perceives clearly]

The expression **opened of the eye** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [whose eye God has opened]

3.q: נְאֻ֤ם בִּלְעָם֙ בְּנ֣⁠וֹ בְעֹ֔ר וּ⁠נְאֻ֥ם הַ⁠גֶּ֖בֶר שְׁתֻ֥ם הָ⁠עָֽיִן
3.note: These two clauses mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in poetry, and follow that approach here and throughout this chapter. Alternate translation: [This is the solemn declaration of Balaam son of Beor, the man whose eye is opened] or [The declaration of Balaam, the son of him, Beor, indeed, the declaration of the man, opened of eye]

4.note: Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the words that God speaks. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the words that God speaks]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the vision that the Almighty reveals. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the vision that the Almighty shows him]

This could mean: (1) Balaam bows down before God in worship. Alternate translation: [prostrating himself] (2) Balaam has fallen into a trance or dream state. Alternate translation: [falling into a trance]

Here Balaam speaks of himself as one whose **eyes** have been **uncovered,** as if a covering that prevented him from perceiving had been removed. He means that God has enabled him to perceive what God reveals to him. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and clearly perceiving what God shows him]

The expression **uncovered of eyes** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God uncovered his eyes]

5.note: Balaam is using a phrase that expresses a strong feeling of admiration. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Your tents are so good]
The pronoun **your** refers to the people of Israel, whom Balaam addresses. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the tents of your people]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [how good are your dwellings, Israel]

6.note: The expression **are stretched out** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [They spread out like wadis]

The point of this comparison is that just as **wadis** are **stretched out** and green with growth, so the settlements of Israel are widespread and flourishing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [They spread out and flourish, widespread and green like river valleys]

The point of this comparison is that just as **gardens upon a river** are lush and well-watered, so the people of Israel are prosperous and thriving. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like well-watered gardens that grow beside a river]

The point of this comparison is that just as **aloes** that **Yahweh has planted** are fragrant and pleasing, so the people of Israel are delightful and firmly established by God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [delightful and firmly established, like aloes that Yahweh has planted]

The point of this comparison is that just as **cedars upon water** are tall, strong, and enduring, so the people of Israel are strong and firmly established. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like cedars growing by the water, they are strong and enduring]

7.note: Here Balaam is speaking of the future prosperity and abundance of Israel as if it were water that would **flow from his buckets**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will have abundant prosperity]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the buckets that belong to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [from the buckets that belong to Israel]

Here, the phrase **his seed** could refer to: (1) seeds from plants that will produce food. Alternate translation: [and his seeds] (2) descendants of the Israelites described as if they were seeds. Alternate translation: [and his offspring]
The pronoun **his** refers to Israel as a nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [from Israel’s buckets]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the king who will rule Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the king who rules Israel]

The expression **will be lifted up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and God will exalt his kingdom]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **kingdom**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the land he rules]

8.note: See how you translated this same phrase in Numbers 23:22. Here, the pronoun **him** could refer to: (1) God. In this case, it means God is like the ox. Alternate translation: [he is like the horns of a wild ox] (2) the Israelites. In this case, it means the Israelites are like the ox. Alternate translation: [they are like the horns of a wild ox]
The pronoun **him** refers to Israel as a nation. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [is bringing Israel out]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [he has strength like the horns of a wild ox for him]

Here Balaam is speaking of Israel conquering enemy nations as if Israel would **devour** them like an animal eating its prey. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He will completely conquer nations, his adversaries]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the nations that oppose Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the nations that oppose him]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the bones that belong to the enemy nations. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the bones of those nations]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the arrows that belong to Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and with the arrows that belong to him]

Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and he will completely destroy them]

9.note: The point of this comparison is that just as a lion and a lioness lie down securely and are dangerous to disturb, so the people of Israel are secure and formidable. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [He lies down securely, as dangerous to disturb as a lion or a lioness]

The terms **bowed down** and **lay down** mean similar things. Balaam is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [He crouched down]

Balaam is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and he lay down like a lioness]

Balaam is using the question form to emphasize that no one dares to rouse or challenge Israel. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [no one would dare to rouse him!]

The expression **blessed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Ones blessing you receive blessing]
The pronoun **you** refers to Israel, whom Balaam now addresses directly. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Ones blessing you Israelites]

The expression **cursed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and ones cursing you receive cursing]

10.note: The author is using **the nose of Balak burned** as a common expression of the culture to mean that Balak became very angry. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Balak became very angry with Balaam]

Clapping the palms together was a symbolic action by which Balak showed his anger and indignation. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [and he clapped his palms together to show his anger]
The author is using the phrase **And Balak said to Balaam** to introduce a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.

Balak is using the possessive form to mean the people who oppose him. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [those hostile to me]

Balak is using **blessing, you have blessed** as a common expression of the culture to emphasize the certainty and completeness of the action. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you have surely blessed them]

11.q: וְ⁠עַתָּ֖ה בְּרַח לְ⁠ךָ֣ אֶל מְקוֹמֶ֑⁠ךָ אָמַ֨רְתִּי֙ כַּבֵּ֣ד אֲכַבֶּדְ⁠ךָ֔ וְ⁠הִנֵּ֛ה מְנָעֲ⁠ךָ֥ יְהוָ֖ה מִ⁠כָּבֽוֹד
11.note: Balak states a result first and then gives the reason for it. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [I said, ‘Honoring, I will honor you,’ but behold, Yahweh has withheld you from honor. So now, flee for yourself to your place]

Balak is using **flee for yourself to your place** as a common expression of the culture to mean “go back home at once.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [hurry back home right away]

Balak is using the possessive form to mean the home where Balaam lives. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the place where you live]

This includes a second-level quotation, something that Balak had said earlier quoted within his present speech. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [I said that I would honor you greatly,]

Balak is using **Honoring, I will honor you** as a common expression of the culture to emphasize how greatly he had intended to reward Balaam. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will surely reward you greatly]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **honor**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [I will cause people to greatly respect you]

12.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֗א גַּ֧ם אֶל מַלְאָכֶ֛י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַ֥חְתָּ אֵלַ֖⁠י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי לֵ⁠אמֹֽר
12.note: What follows is a second-level quotation, the words that Balaam spoke to the messengers. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [Did I not also speak to your messengers whom you sent to me and tell them that]

12.q: הֲ⁠לֹ֗א גַּ֧ם אֶל מַלְאָכֶ֛י⁠ךָ אֲשֶׁר שָׁלַ֥חְתָּ אֵלַ֖⁠י דִּבַּ֥רְתִּי

If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [I also spoke to your messengers]

13.note: This continues a quotation within a quotation. If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [That if Balak gave to me]

Balaam says **the fullness of his house, silver and gold** as an extreme statement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [even all the silver and gold that fills his house]

Here, **the mouth of Yahweh** represents “what Yahweh commands.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [what Yahweh commands]

Balaam is referring to anything he might do by naming two opposite extremes, **good** and **evil**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to do anything at all]
If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **good** and **evil**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what is good or what is bad]

Here, **my own heart** represents “my own will” or “my own initiative.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from my own will]

Balaam is using the possessive form to mean the will that belongs to himself. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [according to my own will]

14.note: Balaam is using the word **Come** to get Balak’s attention before telling him something important, not to tell him to move to a different place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression from your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Listen to me]

Here, **this people** refers to the Israelites, while **your people** refers to the Moabites, Balak’s people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the Israelites will do to your people the Moabites]

Balaam is using **in the end of the days** as a common expression of the culture to mean “in the future” or “in days to come.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in the future]

17.q: דָּרַ֨ךְ כּוֹכָ֜ב מִֽ⁠יַּעֲקֹ֗ב וְ⁠קָ֥ם שֵׁ֨בֶט֙ מִ⁠יִּשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
17.note: Balaam is describing a future event as if it had already happened. He speaks this way to show that the event will certainly take place. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the future tense to express this.

The word translated as **edges** could refer to: (1) the **edges** of a face, or the forehead. The forehead of Moab is a figurative description of the leaders of Moab. Alternate translation: [the forehead of Moab] or [the leaders of Moab] (2) the borders of the territory of **Moab**. In this case, the phrase refers to all the territory of Moab, from one edge to another. Alternate translation: [all the borders of Moab]

The phrase **and destroyed** is a translation of the standard written Hebrew text as we have it today. This reading, however, is rare and difficult. You may want to follow an alternative reading that scholars have proposed, or you may want to follow the major translation in your area. Alternate translation: [and the skull of]

Here Balaam is speaking of a future ruler who will come from Israel as if he were a **scepter**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and a ruler has risen from Israel]

Here, **the edges of Moab** represents “all the territory of Moab.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [all the territory of Moab]
Balaam is speaking as if the people descended from Seth were actually his **sons**. Alternate translation: [Seth’s descendants]

18.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **a possession**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [owned by him]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **strength**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [mighty deeds]

19.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the future ruler who will come from Israel. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And a ruler will rule]

Here, **a survivor** does not refer to a specific person. Balaam means anyone who survives in general. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [every survivor]

This phrase **a city** could refer to: (1) any city that this person conquers. Alternate translation: [from every conquered city] (2) a specific city, perhaps one named “Ir” or “Ar.” Alternate translation: [from the city] or [from Ar] or [from Ir]

Alternate translation: [First of nations to arrive here] (3) being the first to attack the Israelites. Alternate translation: [First of nations to attack Israel]

22.note: The word translated as **Kain** could refer to: (1) an ancestor of the Kenites. See Judges 4:11, where this person may be mentioned. Alternate translation: [you descendants of Kain] (2) Cain, the son of Adam. Alternate translation: [Cain]

Here, the clause **until when Asshur takes you captive** could be: (1) a statement about when the burning takes place. Alternate translation: [to burn until Asshur takes you captive] (2) a rhetorical question about how long Asshur will keep them as captives. Alternate translation: [to burn; until when will Asshur hold you captive?] or [to burn; Asshur will hold you captive for a long time!]

The verb that the ULT translates as **burn** often has this meaning in the Hebrew Bible. However, there is another verb with the same consonants that means “destroy” or “devastate,” and the author may have been using that verb here. If a translation of the Bible exists in your region, you may wish to use the reading that it uses. If a translation of the Bible does not exist in your region, you may wish to use the reading of the ULT. Alternate translation: [to destroy] or [to devastate]
The word translated as **Asshur** could refer to: (1) a tribal group near the Kenites. Alternate translation: [the Asshur tribal group] (2) the Assyrians. Alternate translation: [Assyria]
The pronoun **you** refers to the Kenite people. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [takes you Kenite people captive]
